title: Error during Serialization (`model_dump`)

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: when inference (or the polymorphism trampoline) hits a `__pydantic_serializer__` that is a `MockValSer`, call its `rebuild()` and use the resulting `SchemaSerializer`. Both pass all six independent tests, including the issue's exact example and the function-scope variant. The difference is in how the rebuild resolves names. Patch A threads a `parent_namespace_depth` parameter through `MockValSer.rebuild()` and the `attempt_rebuild` handlers and passes 0 from Rust, so the rebuild uses the class's stored parent namespace rather than walking five Python frames up from a call stack that originates in Rust and has nothing to do with where the class was defined. Patch B calls `rebuild()` with the default depth of 5, which from the Rust call site lands on an arbitrary frame (the Rust-to-Python hop adds the `MockValSer.rebuild` frame, so the usual count is off). A's `test_serialization_inference_unbuildable_model` demonstrates the concrete hazard: a name in the serializing caller's locals must not silently satisfy the forward ref. B's own tests (`test_serialize_instance_of_incomplete_model_by_inference`, `test_polymorphic_serialization_of_incomplete_subclass`) define the forward-referenced class after the model inside a function and expect the Rust-triggered rebuild to find it; that only works if depth 5 happens to hit the test frame, and A's test comment explicitly notes classes must be module-level for this path, so B's tests are at real risk of not passing as written. B does have one nicer edge: when the mock has no rebuild hook it touches `to_python` so the mock raises its own descriptive error instead of the raw cast `TypeError`, whereas A falls through to the `TypeError` in that case. B's trampoline change (only swallowing `AttributeError`) is clean, but A achieves the same via the `Option` return and a shared `py_get_attrs` helper. A's xfail `model_construct` test is unrelated churn but harmless. On correctness at the frame-namespace edge and on tests that are more likely to hold, A is the better fix.

### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hello,

During migration of our code from V1 to V2 we encountered the following error .

```
File "/scratch/envs/pydantic-v2/lib/python3.11/site-packages/pydantic/main.py", line 308, in model_dump
    return self.__pydantic_serializer__.to_python(
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'MockValSer' object cannot be converted to 'SchemaSerializer'
```

After some debugging i found two scenarios where the `model_dump` works

1. when `exclude_unset=True` is set
2. or when one of the fields in the base classes is modified from `default=[]` to `default=None` 

```
step_settings: Union[ StepConstant, StepEstimation] = Field(default=[])
```

if the default of the above field is modified to `None` , then the code works.  

The same works without modifications in V1. I have attached the sample code(apologies for the longer file but i  wasn't able to reliably shorten it) that generates the error. 

NOTE: I have also  tried with `model_rebuild` instead of `update_forward_refs` and `model_dump` instead of `dict`. The code below should work in both V1 and V2.

It would be helpful for debugging if there is a more detailed stack trace for the serialization error. It's not directly clear where the issue lies.

Thanks in advance!

### Example Code

index a99b22ba..45589c96 100644
--- a/pydantic-core/src/serializers/infer.rs
+++ b/pydantic-core/src/serializers/infer.rs
@@ -660,9 +660,26 @@ pub(crate) fn infer_json_key_known<'a, 'py>(
     }
 }
 
+/// Fetch the `__pydantic_serializer__` of `value`.
+///
+/// For models and dataclasses which were not fully defined at creation time, this attribute is a
+/// `MockValSer` placeholder rather than a `SchemaSerializer`; in that case its `rebuild()` method
+/// is called, which either returns the rebuilt `SchemaSerializer` or raises an error explaining
+/// why the class is not fully defined.
 pub(crate) fn get_pydantic_serializer<'py>(value: &Bound<'py, PyAny>) -> PyResult<Bound<'py, SchemaSerializer>> {
     let py = value.py();
     let py_serializer = value.getattr(intern!(py, "__pydantic_serializer__"))?;
+    if py_serializer.is_exact_instance_of::<SchemaSerializer>() {
+        return py_serializer.cast_into_exact().map_err(Into::into);
+    }
+    if let Some(rebuild) = py_serializer.getattr_opt(intern!(py, "rebuild"))? {
+        let rebuilt = rebuild.call0()?;
+        if !rebuilt.is_none() {
+            return rebuilt.cast_into_exact().map_err(Into::into);
+        }
+        // no rebuild was possible; accessing an attribute makes the placeholder raise its own error
+        py_serializer.getattr(intern!(py, "to_python"))?;
+    }
     py_serializer.cast_into_exact().map_err(Into::into)
 }
 
@@ -674,9 +691,8 @@ fn serialize_pydantic_serializable<'py, S: DoSerialize>(
     state: &mut SerializationState<'py>,
     do_serialize: S,
 ) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error> {
-    let py = value.py();
-    let py_serializer = value.getattr(intern!(py, "__pydantic_serializer__"))?;
-    call_pydantic_serializer(py_serializer.cast().map_err(Into::into)?, value, state, do_serialize)
+    let serializer = get_pydantic_serializer(value)?;
+    call_pydantic_serializer(&serializer, value, state, do_serialize)
 }

title: Missing type for PEP695 `TypeAliasType` vs `TypeAlias` when using `TypeAdapter`

judge.reasoning: The issue asks that `TypeAdapter(type=my_type)` for a PEP 695 / `TypeAliasType` alias infer the aliased type, as it does for a plain `TypeAlias`. Patch A addresses this at the root by typing `TypeAdapter.__init__` as `type: TypeForm[T]` (PEP 747), which lets type checkers resolve the alias to `list[dict[str, list[int]]]`. The independent tests confirm this: both alias-inference tests fail on base and pass with A, while they still fail with B (inferred as `Any`). Patch B only adds an overload that collapses any `TypeAliasType` argument to `TypeAdapter[Any]`, which stops the type checker from erroring but discards the type information the issue explicitly wants, so it masks the symptom rather than fixing it. Both patches update the typechecking integration tests; A's `type_adapter.py` changes drop the prior `reportAssertTypeFailure` ignores and assert the correct inferred types for `Annotated`, `Union`, and `|` cases, and add a `type_form.py` covering other `TypeForm` sites. A's scope is much broader (TypeForm across fields, serializers, pipeline, create_model, plus pyrefly config and a pyright version pin in CI), which adds some churn and risk, and it removes the mypy workaround tip from the docs. Those are legitimate scope concerns, but they don't outweigh the fact that A actually resolves the reported behaviour while B does not. A wins on correctness, the primary criterion.

### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There seems to be a difference between the type that is returned from TypeAdapter when used on a PEP695 `TypeAliasType` compared to when it is used on a `TypeAlias`. See example below. When `TypeAdapter` is used on a `TypeAlias`, the correct type is shown. However, when the `TypeAliasType` is used, the type is shown as `TypeAliasType`. This causes the type-checker to see red. 

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import TypeAlias, reveal_type

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

my_type_alias: TypeAlias = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type_alias = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type_alias).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "list[dict[str, list[int]]]"


type my_type = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "TypeAliasType"
```

title: Type variables wrongly replaced when two models share the same type variable instance

judge.reasoning: The issue is that an unparameterized generic model (Model2) whose type variable T is shared with Model1 gets T substituted by Model1[int]'s typevars map. Patch B addresses this at the root: `replace_types` now returns an unparameterized generic model unchanged (treating it as implicitly parameterized with Any), `iter_contained_typevars` no longer reports parameters for unparameterized models, and `get_model_typevars_map` zips the origin's own parameters. Its added tests directly exercise the issue snippet (forward ref, direct reference, list container, Model2[T] still substituted) and all five independent tests fail on base and pass on B. Patch A instead changes which namespace/typevars map is used when rebuilding fields of a parametrized generic during schema generation. That fixes adjacent forward-ref problems (and un-xfails two tests), but it does not touch `replace_types`, so Model2 still has T replaced when Model1[int] is built; all five independent tests still raise ValidationError on A, and A's own nested-model test only covers a non-generic Inner, not the issue's shared-TypeVar scenario. Patch B does carry extra semantic churn (Model[T] is no longer `Model`, a new PydanticUndefinedAnnotation raise during self-referencing definition, updated existing test expectations), which adds some risk, but it is the only patch that resolves the reported behaviour.

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar

T = TypeVar('T')

    t: T

Model1[int].model_validate({'m2': {'t': 'not_an_int'}})
# raises a ValidationError, shouldn't
```

title: Bug: false `Unexpected keyword argument` in pydantic.mypy plugin (in very specific case)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches attack the same root cause: a subclass's transform runs while the plugin has started but not finished the base model (deferred because of unresolved forward refs in an import cycle), so the base's fields and extra='forbid' config are missing from the generated __init__/model_construct signatures. Both mark the base's TypeInfo metadata at the start of transform and make the subclass defer when it sees a marked-but-unfinished base, falling through on the final iteration. On the core scenario they are equivalent.

B is slightly more robust in the details. It removes the 'incomplete' marker when the transform completes (and explicitly on the final iteration when fields can't resolve), so the check is a true in-progress flag rather than A's permanent tag combined with an absence-of-METADATA_KEY test; that also covers the case where a base is re-transformed after its metadata was already stored. B calls defer() right where it returns (None, None), keeping the deferral paired with the wait, whereas A relies on the caller to defer. Neither leaves stale state in the cache in practice.

Tests: A adds a compact two-module cycle test that would fail before (missing inherited 'name') and asserts the real error ('nam') still fires, which is adequate, but it also edits pyproject's codespell ignore list purely to accommodate the test's typo, which is unrelated churn. B reproduces the issue's actual structure (forbid base, Node with Annotated tagged union, Circle/Square in sibling modules, TYPE_CHECKING imports) and checks valid inherited-field calls produce no errors, that extra='forbid' still rejects unknown kwargs, and that model_construct gets the inherited/own field types right. One oddity in B's test is that Square derives from Node while Circle derives from BaseShape, but that doesn't weaken it. Independent tests were all skipped and provide no signal.

Overall B wins on marginally better state handling and a more faithful, broader test, with A carrying a small unrelated config change.

title: AssertionError for the mypy plugin if type variables are defined before their bound

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: before generating methods, check whether the class's type variables still contain placeholder types (the forward-referenced bound) and defer so the generated `self`/return types do not carry placeholders into the final iteration. Both pass all four independent tests. Differences: (1) Control flow. Patch A mirrors the existing field-placeholder check exactly: it defers when not in the final iteration and returns False either way, so methods are never generated with placeholder types. Patch B only returns early when it can defer; on the final iteration it falls through and generates methods with placeholders still present, which is the very state that produced the internal error. That is an edge case, but it is an inconsistency with the surrounding pattern and a residual risk. (2) Coverage. Patch A explicitly checks bound, default and constraint values; Patch B relies on mypy's `has_placeholder` type visitor, which also recurses into those for TypeVarType, so B is not less correct there, just more implicit. (3) Patch A also fixes a latent bug in `add_method`: plugin-generated classmethods are stored as a `Decorator` symbol while only the `FuncDef` lives in the class body, so the existing cleanup never removed stale generated classmethods on re-runs. This is adjacent but directly relevant once the transformer can now be re-run after deferring, and it is small and low risk. (4) Tests. Patch A adds a dedicated regression module exercising bound, constraints and default TypeVars plus assert_type checks on instantiation and model_construct; Patch B adds a minimal bound-only case to an existing module (with double-quoted strings inconsistent with the file's style). A's tests are broader and would fail before the fix. Overall A is the more careful, consistent and better-tested fix.

### Description

Running `mypy` with the `pydantic.mypy` plugin enabled fails with an error if it encounters a `BaseModel` with a bound `TypeVar`, where the type variable is defined _before_ its `bound`. (See the minimal example below for an illustration) With the `pydantic.mypy` plugin disabled, type checking is successful.

Error details:

AssertionError: Must not defer during final iteration

In my experience, it is quite common to define type variables at the top of the module, see for example the [mypy docs on Generics](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generics.html).

title: Some Field attributes lost in JSON schema when using RootModel

judge.reasoning: Both patches add examples, deprecated, and title from the root field in `model_schema` and pass all independent tests. Patch A is more correct at the edges. It uses `root_field._attributes_set` to apply only an explicitly set field title, so a config `field_title_generator` (which mutates `FieldInfo.title` during schema generation) does not replace the model's class name with 'ROOT'; Patch B reads `.title` directly and would regress that case, and A adds a test for it. A also handles `deprecated=''` like the existing field-level code (`bool(deprecated) or deprecated == ''`) and uses `setdefault` for `deprecated`, while B unconditionally assigns. A's precedence (config title > explicit field title > model_title_generator > class name) is defensible and tested; B puts model_title_generator above field title, also defensible, but untested. A's tests are broader: Annotated and assigned forms, deprecation message string, deprecated=False, nested `$defs` consistency, config-title precedence, and title-generator interaction. B's tests cover the basic cases only. Scope and craft are comparable, with A slightly cleaner by hoisting `root_field` once and reusing it for the description branch.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When declaring a RootModel and adding a `Field` annotation to the `root` property that includes `examples`, those `examples` are not part of the generated JSON schema. This also applies to the `deprecated` attribute. The `title` attribute is also not applied or it is overwritten by the class name of the root model class. 

Most other attributes, such as `pattern` or `description` are exposed as expected. Furthermore, placing `examples` in `json_schema_extra` also works as expected.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import RootModel, Field

class Foo(RootModel):
    root: Annotated[str, Field(examples=["foo", "bar"], deprecated=True)]

print(Foo.model_json_schema())  # does not include examples or deprecated.
```

title: Add `FastMCP` and MCP's `python-sdk` to third-party tests

judge.reasoning: Both patches add the two requested jobs with the same trigger conditions, checkout pattern, pinned action SHAs, and wiring into create-issue-on-failure, so on the core ask they are comparable. Patch A stays strictly within scope: two new jobs that mirror the existing FastDepends job structure (uv sync, uninstall pydantic/pydantic-core, install both from the checked-out monorepo, list deps, run pytest), plus the needs/if updates. Its FastMCP job skips integration tests and its MCP job uses --frozen, which is reasonable. Patch B's new jobs show more targeted investigation (unit-only markers copied from FastMCP's own CI, unsetting FORCE_COLOR for CLI output assertions, MCP_EXAMPLES_SMOKE gate, -n auto, inline-snapshot disabled), which may make the FastMCP job less flaky. However, B also makes many unrelated changes to existing jobs: replacing the ODMantic actions/checkout with a raw git clone, appending 'tests/' to Beanie/Polar/Django Ninja/FastDepends/ODMantic commands (the ODMantic line now passes 'tests' twice), adding a Redis service to the Polar job, swapping Dify's uv install for setup-uv and replacing Dify's upstream test script with a direct pytest invocation. These touch jobs the issue never mentions, change how Dify tests are selected, and obscure the actual fix in the diff; per the scope rule they count against B because they add risk. B also installs only pydantic (not pydantic-core) from the checkout and uses a narrower FastMCP matrix (3.10 and 3.13 only), while A installs both packages from the monorepo like a true main-branch test and covers 3.10-3.13 for both projects. Given that neither can be independently verified, A's focused, convention-consistent change is the safer and better-scoped fix.

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead regex unsupported by pydantic-core

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the independent round-trip tests pass, but they do so differently. Patch B fixes the root cause: it rewrites the decimal pattern without look-around while preserving the existing semantics (sign, leading/trailing zeros not counted, all four max_digits/decimal_places cases), and it explicitly solves the large-constraint compile-size problem via the halving split in shared_digits_with_dot, which it verifies with max_digits=1000 tests through pydantic-core. Its new tests directly exercise the issue scenario (TypeAdapter with StringConstraints built from the emitted pattern) and cross-check Python re vs pydantic-core results over a value table, so they fail on base and pass after. Patch A resolves the issue largely by removing the pattern from the default JSON schema entirely and moving pattern generation behind a new opt-in GenerateJsonSchema.get_decimal_pattern/build_decimal_pattern API. That is a user-visible behavior change well beyond the ask (consumers relying on the emitted pattern lose it), a sizable redesign (new public methods, serialization-mode patterns, exponent and inf/nan handling, docs rewrite), and its tests mostly validate the new opt-in builder rather than the issue's round-trip through pydantic-core. A's opt-in max_digits-only validation pattern also enumerates O(n) alternatives whose compiled size grows roughly quadratically, which B deliberately avoided. B is the tighter, lower-risk, directly tested fix; A's extra scope adds risk and obscures the fix rather than earning credit.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

  Pydantic v2 emits a JSON schema for Decimal fields that includes a regex pattern with a negative lookahead `((?!...))`. This pattern cannot be compiled by `pydantic-core`'s Rust regex crate, which does not support look-around assertions.

  This means the JSON schema pydantic produces for Decimal cannot be round-tripped back through pydantic's own validation  e.g. constructing a `TypeAdapter` with `StringConstraints(pattern=...)` using the emitted pattern fails with a `SchemaError`.

  This is a practical problem for any tooling that reconstructs pydantic types from emitted JSON schemas (e.g. MCP structured content parsing via FastMCP).


### Example Code

```Python
"""Minimal reproduction: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead unsupported by pydantic-core.

Pydantic generates a JSON schema for Decimal fields with a regex pattern that uses
a negative lookahead (?!...). When that schema is round-tripped back through pydantic
(e.g. via TypeAdapter with StringConstraints), pydantic-core's Rust regex engine
rejects it because it does not support look-around assertions.
"""

from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints, TypeAdapter


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    amount: Decimal


def test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core():
    schema = MyModel.model_json_schema()

    # Decimal emits an anyOf with a string variant carrying the pattern
    string_variant = next(v for v in schema['properties']['amount']['anyOf'] if v.get('type') == 'string')
    pattern = string_variant['pattern']

    # The emitted pattern contains a negative lookahead:
    assert '(?!' in pattern

    # Feeding it back into StringConstraints fails with:
    #   SchemaError: regex parse error: look-around ... is not supported
    ConstrainedStr = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=pattern)]
    TypeAdapter(ConstrainedStr)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core()
```

+# Decimal JSON Schema pattern utilities.
+# Note: while we could use `\d` to represent digits (`Decimal` objects allow Unicode decimal digits), we use [0-9] instead:
+# - to reduce complexity (`\d` expands to a large set, and with `max_digits`/`decimal_places` constraints set, it can blow
+#   the compile limit on some engines).
+# - [0-9] is a portable pattern (e.g. `\d` is equivalent to `[0-9]` in ECMA (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Regular_expressions/Character_class_escape#d)
+#   while it allows any Unicode decimal digit in Python.
+
+
+def _repeat(atom: str, min_count: int, max_count: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex repetition of `atom` between `min_count` and `max_count` times (inclusive), using the shortest quantifier."""
+    if min_count > max_count or max_count == 0:
+        return ''
+    if min_count == max_count:
+        return atom if min_count == 1 else f'{atom}{{{min_count}}}'
+    if (min_count, max_count) == (0, 1):
+        return f'{atom}?'
+    return f'{atom}{{{min_count},{max_count}}}'
+
+
+def _int_range_pattern(max_value: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex matching the integers between 1 and `max_value` (inclusive), without leading zeros."""
+    digits = str(max_value)
+    length = len(digits)
+    alts: list[str] = [f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", k - 1, k - 1)}' for k in range(1, length)]
+    for i, char in enumerate(digits):
+        d = int(char)
+        low = 1 if i == 0 else 0
+        high = d if i == length - 1 else d - 1
+        if high >= low:
+            char_class = str(low) if low == high else f'[{low}-{high}]'
+            alts.append(f'{digits[:i]}{char_class}{_repeat("[0-9]", length - i - 1, length - i - 1)}')
+    return alts[0] if len(alts) == 1 else f'(?:{"|".join(alts)})'
+
+
+def _decimal_validation_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'validation'` mode."""
+
+    number = r'(?:[0-9]+\.?[0-9]*|\.[0-9]+)'  # e.g. 1, 1., .5
+    exponent = r'[eE][+-]?[0-9]+'  # e.g. e5, E5, e-7
+    # e.g. Infinity, inf, NaN, sNaN, NaN123 (case-insensitive). Spelled out explicitly, as inline flags
+    # aren't supported by all regular expression engines:
+    non_finite = r'|[iI][nN][fF](?:[iI][nN][iI][tT][yY])?|[sS]?[nN][aA][nN][0-9]*' if allow_inf_nan else ''
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        return rf'^[+-]?(?:{number}(?:{exponent})?{non_finite})$'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        # If `decimal_places > max_digits`, no whole digits are allowed and `max_digits` bounds the decimal places:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, whole)}' if whole else '0+'
+        opt_int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole)}'
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'{int_part}(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'{opt_int_part}{frac_part}']
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}' if max_digits else '0+'
+        alts.append(rf'{int_part}(?:\.0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            rf'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", whole, whole)}\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits - whole)}0*'
+            for whole in range(max_digits)
+        ] or [r'0*\.0+']
+    else:
+        assert decimal_places is not None
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, decimal_places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, decimal_places)}0*' if decimal_places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'[0-9]+(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'[0-9]*{frac_part}']
+
+    alts.append(f'{number}{exponent}')
+    return rf'^[+-]?(?:{"|".join(alts)}{non_finite})$'

+def _decimal_serialization_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'serialization'` mode.
+
+    Decimals are serialized using `str()`, producing either:
+
+    - The plain notation (`'123.45'`), when the exponent is lower than or equal to 0 and the adjusted
+      exponent is greater than or equal to -6.
+    - The scientific notation otherwise (`'1E+3'`, `'1.5E-7'`, `'0E-10'`), with a single digit before
+      the optional decimal point and an always signed exponent.
+
+    Trailing zeros of the decimal part are preserved by `str()`, but aren't counted by the validation logic.
+    """
+
+    def frac_part(places: int) -> str:
+        return rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+
+    # Plain notation:
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'(?:0|[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole - 1)})' if whole else '0'
+        alts.append(f'{int_part}(?:{frac_part(places)})?')
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        alts.append(rf'0(?:\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", whole - 1, whole - 1)}(?:{frac_part(max_digits - whole)})?'
+            for whole in range(1, max_digits + 1)
+        ]
+    elif decimal_places is not None:
+        alts.append(f'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:{frac_part(decimal_places)})?')
+    else:
+        alts.append(r'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?')
+
+    # Zero with an exponent (e.g. `'0E-10'`), which normalizes to zero and thus satisfies any constraint:
+    alts.append(r'0E[+-][1-9][0-9]*')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a positive exponent `k` (e.g. `'1.5E+3'`): the value has `k + 1` whole digits
+    # and no decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_exponent = max_digits - (decimal_places or 0) - 1
+        if max_exponent >= 1:
+            alts.append(rf'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+{_int_range_pattern(max_exponent)}')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a negative exponent `k` (`k >= 7`, e.g. `'1.5E-7'`): the value has no whole digits,
+    # and `k` + (the number of significant decimal digits of the coefficient) decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E-[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_places = min(c for c in (max_digits, decimal_places) if c is not None)
+        alts += [f'[1-9](?:{frac_part(max_places - k)})?E-{k}' for k in range(7, max_places + 1)]
+
+    if allow_inf_nan:
+        # `str()` produces `'Infinity'`, `'NaN'` and `'sNaN'` (with an optional payload):
+        alts += ['Infinity', 's?NaN[0-9]*']
+
+    return rf'^-?(?:{"|".join(alts)})$'

title: Allow arbitrary core schemas for serialization

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make pydantic-core build a serializer from an arbitrary core schema via `CombinedSerializer::build`, and both pass the independent core-schema tests. The decisive differences are in design and completeness.

Patch A overloads the existing `serialization` key so any core schema is accepted directly. This creates a real ambiguity it has to document away: `function-plain`/`function-wrap` validator schemas collide with the function ser-schema types and cannot be used, which is why A needs the `as_ser_schema` shim in pydantic. The typing change is also a hack: `SerSchema` becomes a string alias containing `CoreSchema` (recursive), and two other aliases get `Union[...]` with `noqa` comments because the alias raises `TypeError` when evaluated. Most importantly, A does not actually resolve the issue on the pydantic side: `ValidateAs` still emits the identity wrap serializer (the TODO is merely reworded), the new `as_ser_schema` helper is added and unit-tested but never used, and the other call sites named in the issue (`PlainValidator`, `InstanceOf`, `SkipValidation`, mapping schemas) are untouched. The independent `ValidateAs` tests fail on A for exactly this reason, and the diff confirms it.

Patch B adds an explicit `SchemaSerSchema` (`type='schema'`) with a `schema_ser_schema()` constructor, mirroring the existing `model_ser_schema` convention. It has no type collision, no typing hacks, a clear error path (`Error building \`schema\` serializer`), and it is wired through `GenerateJsonSchema.ser_schema` for serialization-mode JSON schema. It then replaces the identity-wrap workaround in every place the issue points at (`ValidateAs`, `PlainValidator`, `InstanceOf`, `SkipValidation`, the `lax_or_strict` mapping path). Tests cover the core behavior (nested `serialization`, definitions/refs, models, missing-schema error) and the pydantic integrations, including assertions that no wrap function remains and that serialization JSON schemas are correct. All independent tests pass on B.

B resolves the issue at the root and end to end with a cleaner, less risky design; A leaves the issue's primary example unfixed and introduces typing and semantic ambiguity.

issue_md:
As per the TODO in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13487:

There is currently no way to tell `pydantic-core` "serialize this value using this core schema". `Ser`Schema is:

```python
SerSchema = Union[
    SimpleSerSchema,
    PlainSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    WrapSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    FormatSerSchema,
    ToStringSerSchema,
    ModelSerSchema,
]
```

The only member that expresses "use this schema" is `SimpleSerSchema`, and it does not take a schema at all, only a name from a closed literal:

```python
ExpectedSerializationTypes = Literal[
    'none', 'int', 'bool', 'float', 'str', 'bytes', 'bytearray', 'list', 'tuple',
    'set', 'frozenset', 'generator', 'dict', 'datetime', 'date', 'time', 'timedelta',
    'url', 'multi-host-url', 'json', 'uuid', 'any',
]

class SimpleSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
    type: Required[ExpectedSerializationTypes]
```

So an arbitrary schema (a model, a dataclass, `list[int]`, a TypedDict, anything constructed by the schema generator) cannot be used directly. Every place in Pydantic that needs it works around the gap the same way: it wraps the schema in a wrap serializer whose function is the identity, purely so the schema can ride along in the `schema` argument.

From `ValidateAs.__get_pydantic_core_schema__()`:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/27f95c789b20aa23306e5ce559327db0e9a10a6e/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L911-L917

     return ModelSerSchema(type='model', cls=cls, schema=schema)
 
 
+class SchemaSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
+    type: Required[Literal['schema']]
+    schema: Required[CoreSchema]
+
+
+def schema_ser_schema(schema: CoreSchema) -> SchemaSerSchema:
+    """
+    Returns a schema for serialization using an arbitrary core schema.
+
+    The value is serialized as if it was described by `schema`, independently of the schema used for validation:
+
+    ```py
+    from pydantic_core import SchemaSerializer, core_schema
+
+    list_of_bytes = core_schema.list_schema(core_schema.bytes_schema())
+    ser_schema = core_schema.schema_ser_schema(list_of_bytes)
+    schema = core_schema.any_schema(serialization=ser_schema)
+    v = SchemaSerializer(schema)
+    assert v.to_python([b'a'], mode='json') == ['a']
+    ```
+
+    Args:
+        schema: The core schema to use to serialize the value
+    """
+    return SchemaSerSchema(type='schema', schema=schema)
+
+

+def as_ser_schema(schema: CoreSchema) -> core_schema.SerSchema:
+    """Return a schema suitable for the `'serialization'` key of a core schema, from an arbitrary core schema.
+
+    Any core schema can be used as a serialization schema, except `'function-plain'` and `'function-wrap'`
+    schemas, as these types are already used by the plain and wrap serializer *function* schemas.
+    For these, mimic what pydantic-core would do if they were used as the *main* schema:
+
+    - if the function schema has a `'serialization'` schema, use it.
+    - otherwise, a `'function-plain'` schema is serialized as `'any'`, and a `'function-wrap'` schema
+      is serialized using its inner schema.
+
+    Note that `schema` is expected to be a *core* schema (e.g. as returned by the schema generator),
+    not an existing `'serialization'` schema.
+    """
+    if schema['type'] == 'function-plain' or schema['type'] == 'function-wrap':
+        if (ser_schema := schema.get('serialization')) is not None:
+            return ser_schema
+        if schema['type'] == 'function-plain':
+            return core_schema.any_schema()
+        return as_ser_schema(schema['schema'])
+    return schema

title: model_dump(exclude=...) is silently ignored in python mode when a wrap model_serializer is gated with when_used="json"

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the same root cause in the same place: when the serializer function is gated off (when_used='json' in python mode), the fallback serializer was wrapped in a scoped empty IncludeExclude, so caller include/exclude was discarded. Both now forward the caller's include/exclude to the fallback path and only clear it when the function actually ran; independent tests pass equally for both across json and json-unless-none, include and exclude, nested and ungated comparisons. The difference is in tests and craft. Patch B's tests are considerably more thorough: it adds a parametrized pydantic-core test (plain and wrap, json and json-unless-none) at the layer where the fix lives, plus pydantic-level tests for wrap, plain, and nested Annotated serializers with nested include/exclude, and checks model_dump_json too. Patch A adds a single test covering plain and wrap with when_used='json' only, with no nested or json-unless-none coverage and nothing in pydantic-core's own suite. On craft, A adds a new public accessor that clones the IncludeExclude on every fallback call and rebuilds a scoped state unnecessarily; B passes the existing state straight through to the fallback and scopes only in the function-used branch, which is clearer about intent and avoids the needless clone, at the cost of some verbosity. Neither patch adds unrelated churn. B is the better fix on tests and marginally on craft.

title: Cannot create `defauldict` field with `dict` value type

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause identically: adding `dict: dict` (and `frozenset: frozenset`) to the allowed-default-types mapping, and all independent tests pass on both. Patch A is a minimal two-line change plus focused tests covering bare and parametrized dict/frozenset values and the issue's exact model. Patch B does the same but also hoists the mapping to module level and adds speculative, version-gated code for Python 3.15 that references an undefined name `frozendict` (suppressed with `noqa: F821`) and silently remaps `collections.abc.Mapping` to `frozendict` on that version. That is unrelated to the issue, changes existing behaviour (Mapping-valued defaultdicts would yield immutable values on 3.15), and risks a NameError at import time if `frozendict` is not a builtin there; the test file carries the same speculative reference. B's correction of 'keys' to 'values' in the error message and its deterministic ordering of the allowed-types list are small genuine improvements, and its parametrized test rewrite is reasonable, but they do not outweigh the risk introduced by the 3.15 branch. A resolves the issue cleanly with no added risk.

title: Memory leak: transient models using Enum methods or Field(exclude_if=...) survive GC

judge.reasoning: Both patches add the three traversal edges the issue identifies (SerField.serialization_exclude_if, EnumSerializer.class, EnumValidator.lookup for all four variants) and both pass every independent test, so correctness on the reported scenarios is equal. The differences are in tests and scope. Patch A rewrites the existing GC tests unrelated to the fix: it deletes the free-threaded xfail markers from test_gc_schema_serializer and test_gc_schema_validator, drops the sys/is_free_threaded imports, and renames the class attributes used in those tests. That is unexplained churn that could turn previously-tolerated free-threaded leaks into CI failures. Its new tests are reasonable (they create class<->serializer/validator cycles that would not collect before the fix), though the enum tests only exercise the str sub_type. Patch B keeps the existing tests intact, adds a reusable holder-based harness that covers all four enum validator sub_types plus the serializer and exclude_if paths, and adds an end-to-end test in tests/test_main.py that mirrors the issue's transient-module reproduction (enum with method, Field(exclude_if), computed_field(exclude_if)). B also fixes closely related missing edges of the same kind (ComputedField.serialization_exclude_if, GeneralFieldsSerializer.extra_serializer, extras validators, LiteralLookup unhashable values), each with its own regression test; these are mechanical one-line traversal additions with no behavioral risk and the harness confirms they compiled and ran. Given equal root-cause correctness, B wins on test quality and on avoiding A's unrelated edits to existing tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Transient `BaseModel` classes are not collected when either:
* A model field references an `Enum` whose class defines a Python method.
* A model field uses `Field(exclude_if=<Python callable>)`.

After the defining module is removed from `sys.modules` and every ordinary strong reference is dropped, weak references to the model and enum classes remain alive after repeated full `gc.collect()` calls. Repeating this construction in disposable module namespaces causes linear memory growth.

Controls using an enum without methods or a field without `exclude_if` are collected normally.

I encountered this in combination with a Temporal workflow sandbox. With a large interconnected model graph and high volume Temporal workflows this can result in multi-GiB process growth relatively quickly.

The likely cause is missing `PyGcTraverse` edges for Python objects held by pydantic-core:
* `SerField` owns `serialization_exclude_if`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/fields.rs#L26-L38
* `EnumSerializer` owns `class`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/enum_.rs
* Each `EnumValidator<T>` owns `lookup`, but traverses only `class` and `missing`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/validators/enum_.rs

Traversing `py_schema` does not compensate for another unreported direct reference: CPython’s collector accounts for every actual strong edge individually.

I tested a temporary build from Pydantic `main` at `c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c`. Adding only these traversal edges made all objects in the reproduction collectible:
* Add `serialization_exclude_if` to `SerField` traversal.
* Add `class` to `EnumSerializer` traversal.
* Add `lookup` to every `EnumValidator<T>` traversal.

For the enum case, changing only the serializer or only the validator was insufficient; both missing edges were required.

This appears related to earlier missing-traversal fixes such as:

* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5136
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/787
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1100

I would be happy to submit a focused patch.

(please note that this analysis was LLM assisted)

### Example Code

```Python
import gc
import sys
import types
import weakref

def transient_module(name, source, class_names):
    module = types.ModuleType(name)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    exec(compile(source, f"<{name}>", "exec"), module.__dict__)
    refs = tuple(
        weakref.ref(module.__dict__[class_name])
        for class_name in class_names
    )
    del sys.modules[name]
    del module
    return refs

enum_ref, enum_model_ref = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_enum_gc_repro",
    """
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Membership(str, Enum):
    FULL = "full"
    def label(self) -> str:
        return self.value
class Model(BaseModel):
    membership: Membership
""",
    ("Membership", "Model"),
)

(exclude_if_model_ref,) = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_exclude_if_gc_repro",
    """
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Model(BaseModel):
    value: int = Field(exclude_if=lambda value: False)
""",
    ("Model",),
)

for _ in range(5):
    gc.collect()

# All three should be False because no intentional strong references remain.
print("enum alive:", enum_ref() is not None)
print("enum model alive:", enum_model_ref() is not None)
print("exclude_if model alive:", exclude_if_model_ref() is not None)
```

title: JSON schema discriminator mapping uses Python-style `True`/`False` keys for `bool` discriminators

judge.reasoning: Both patches change `GenerateJsonSchema.tagged_union_schema` to emit `true`/`false` keys for bool discriminators, and both pass the core scenarios from the issue (plain Literal[True]/Literal[False], TypeAdapter annotated union, mixed bool/string literals). The difference is ordering relative to the existing Enum normalization. Patch A applies the bool check after `k = k.value`, so an Enum whose member values are True/False also yields `true`/`false`. Patch B uses `elif isinstance(k, bool)`, so once a key is an Enum it is unwrapped to a raw bool and then falls through to `str(k)`, producing `True`/`False` again. The issue explicitly points at the Enum-to-value normalization as the path bool keys sit next to, and an Enum with bool values serializes to JSON `true`/`false` just like a bare bool, so B leaves a directly adjacent instance of the same bug in place. The independent test for that case confirms it: A passes, B fails with the old `'False'`/`'True'` keys. On tests, A adds two targeted tests (plain bool and bool-valued Enum) that would fail before and pass after; B adds one full-schema assertion that covers the plain case well but not the Enum case. Scope and craft are comparable: both are small, localized edits with reasonable comments, and A's inline conditional is slightly denser but clear. A is the more complete root-cause fix.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When a discriminated union uses a `bool` discriminator (`Literal[True]` / `Literal[False]`), the generated JSON schema's `discriminator.mapping` uses the Python string representations `"True"` and `"False"` as keys:

```json
"discriminator": {
    "mapping": {"False": "#/$defs/Disabled", "True": "#/$defs/Enabled"},
    "propertyName": "enabled"
}
```

Per the [OpenAPI discriminator specification](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0#discriminator-object), mapping keys must match the serialized payload value of the discriminator property. For a boolean property, that value serializes to JSON `true`/`false`, so the keys should be `"true"` and `"false"`. Tooling that resolves the mapping against the payload (code generators, validators such as openapi-generator or Redocly) fails to match either variant.

Expected:

```json
"mapping": {"false": "#/$defs/Disabled", "true": "#/$defs/Enabled"}
```

Note that `Enum` discriminator keys are already normalized to their value (`k.value`) before stringification in `GenerateJsonSchema.tagged_union_schema`; `bool` keys just fall through to `str(k)`.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Enabled(BaseModel):
    enabled: Literal[True]
    config: str


class Disabled(BaseModel):
    enabled: Literal[False]


class Model(BaseModel):
    setting: Enabled | Disabled = Field(discriminator='enabled')


print(Model.model_json_schema()['properties']['setting']['discriminator'])
# {'propertyName': 'enabled', 'mapping': {'True': '#/$defs/Enabled', 'False': '#/$defs/Disabled'}}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
             pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=debug pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.15 (main, Apr 14 2026, 14:28:36) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
                     platform: Linux-6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.41
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.15.0
```

title: TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' in match_type for PEP 695 aliases with a ParamSpec (regression in 2.14.0b1)

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the reported crash and pass all six independent tests. Patch B guards the `DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)` lookup with `try/except TypeError`, which is exactly one of the fixes the issue suggests, is self-contained, and carries a clear comment. Its tests reproduce the issue's scenario directly (a `TypeAliasType` with a `ParamSpec` parameterized as `Alias[[], int]`, both optional and non-optional fields, plus a `TypeAdapter`), so they would fail on base and pass after. It also fixes a second hashing site in `_path_schema` (`{str, bytes}` set membership) with a dedicated test; this is adjacent but low risk and covered. Patch A instead switches to an identity-keyed `DEPRECATED_ALIASES_IDS` table, which is a reasonable design but requires bumping the `typing-inspection` minimum to a new release, adding dependency friction and risk outside the issue's ask. Its single test uses an unrelated construction (`list[Annotated[int, Meta()]]` with `__hash__ = None`) rather than the ParamSpec alias from the issue, and the test name contains a typo. On correctness they are equivalent; on tests and scope B is stronger.

issue_md:
Reported downstream in Giskard-AI/giskard#2719 (breaks `import giskard.checks`); repro and analysis below. The report was drafted jointly with @davidberenstein1957, who invited it to be filed upstream as-is.

### Description

`_generate_schema.match_type` added an unguarded dict lookup in 2.14 that assumes the annotation object is hashable. It is not, for a PEP 695 type alias with a `ParamSpec` parameterized by an empty list. Schema building for any model containing such an annotation crashes.

This is a regression: the same code builds fine on 2.13.4.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel

type Alias[**P, R] = Any

class M(BaseModel):
    f: Alias[[], int] | None = None
```

Raises immediately at class-definition time:

```
File ".../pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py", line 1127, in match_type
    if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

### Mechanism

`Alias[[], int]` is a `types.GenericAlias` whose `__args__` is `([], int)`. Hashing the alias hashes that tuple, which contains a `list` — so it is unhashable. The line at `_generate_schema.py:1127`

```python
if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

calls `.get(obj)` without checking that `obj` can be hashed. `dict.get` propagates the `TypeError` rather than treating an unhashable key as absent.

### Suggested fix

Guard the lookup, e.g.

```python
if origin is not None and isinstance(obj, Hashable) and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

or wrap it in `try/except TypeError`. An unhashable object cannot be a `DEPRECATED_ALIASES` key by construction, so skipping the lookup is always correct.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

- pydantic 2.14.0b1 (fails) / 2.13.4 (works)
- Python 3.12.13
- Reproduced on Linux and macOS

### Real-world impact

Hit in [giskard-oss](https://github.com/Giskard-AI/giskard-oss), where `type GeneratorType[**P, R, S] = ...` parameterized as `GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]` makes `import giskard.checks` fail outright under 2.14.0b1. Instrumenting `match_type` confirms the offending object:

```
OFFENDING obj  = GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]
OFFENDING type = <class 'types.GenericAlias'>
OFFENDING args = ([], InputType, None)
```

There is no workaround on the library side short of pinning `pydantic<2.14` (done in Giskard-AI/giskard#2752), which is what downstream has had to do.

title: Runtime by_name/by_alias arguments dropped by model_validator(mode="wrap")

judge.reasoning: The Rust change is identical in both patches: InternalValidator now captures extra.by_alias/by_name at construction and forwards them in both validate() and validate_assignment() instead of hardcoding None. This is the root cause (the wrap-validator handler and generator paths rebuilt Extra with the runtime flags discarded), and independent tests confirm both patches fix every scenario including JSON and nested models. The only difference is field placement (cosmetic) and tests. Patch A's tests exercise the issue's axis more completely: python/json/strings entry points for the wrap model validator, a wrap field validator around a nested model, validate_assignment (the second code path touched by the fix), and the Iterable/generator path that shares InternalValidator. Each of these would fail on base and pass after the fix. Patch B covers the model-wrap and field-wrap cases, but its second test checks context/strict/extra/from_attributes forwarding, which already worked before the change and so does not exercise the fix. B's test is adequate; A's is more targeted to the paths the diff actually modifies, including validate_assignment which B never tests. Narrow win for A on test coverage; correctness and scope are equal.

### Initial Checks

### Description

The `handler` passed to a wrap-mode model validator appears to silently drop the passed-in `by_name`/`by_alias` arguments from the top-level `validate_python` methods.


### Example Code

```Python

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter, ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler, model_validator

CFG = {"alias_generator": lambda s: s.replace("_", "-"), "validate_by_name": True}

class Plain(BaseModel):
    model_config = CFG
    build_depends: list[str] = []

class Wrapped(BaseModel):
    model_config = CFG
    build_depends: list[str] = []

    @model_validator(mode="wrap")
    @classmethod
    def _noop(cls, data, handler: ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler) -> Self:
        return handler(data)

data = {"build_depends": ["x"]}  # field name, not the alias
print(TypeAdapter(Plain).validate_python(data, by_alias=True, by_name=False))    # build_depends=[]    correct
print(TypeAdapter(Wrapped).validate_python(data, by_alias=True, by_name=False))  # build_depends=['x'] wrong

title: `TypeAdapter` config not used for JSON Schema generation

judge.reasoning: Both patches apply the same core fix for the single-adapter case: pushing the TypeAdapter's config onto the JSON schema generator's config wrapper stack before `generate()`. That resolves the exact snippet in the issue, and the independent tests confirm both pass the direct bytes/list[bytes] scenarios. Patch B goes further on the same root cause in ways that matter: (1) `TypeAdapter.json_schemas()` is left untouched by Patch A, so multiple adapters passed together still ignore their configs, which is the very bug reported, just via the sibling API; B threads per-input configs through `generate_definitions()` with a length check. (2) B makes config-less TypedDicts and stdlib dataclasses nested inside the adapter inherit the adapter config during JSON schema generation, mirroring core schema generation. This is justified rather than speculative: B's test shows `dump_json` already serializes such nested bytes as base64 under the adapter config, so on Patch A the JSON schema would contradict actual serialization output. The independent tests show exactly this split: A fails the nested TypedDict, nested dataclass, and `json_schemas` cases, B passes all six. B's change of `_get_typed_dict_config` to return `None` is safe because `ConfigWrapperStack.push(None)` is a no-op, and the `config or {}` fallback preserves `_update_class_schema`'s contract. B's tests are also more thorough (several config keys, both modes, nested classes, `json_schemas`), all of which fail before and pass after. A's single test is adequate but narrow. B's extra surface (`_definitions_input_configs` attribute set externally on the generator) is slightly awkward design, but it is small, commented, and validated, and does not outweigh A leaving real instances of the reported behaviour broken.

title: `populate_by_name` (and implicit `validate_by_name` when `validate_by_alias=False`) is ignored by `@validate_call`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way in effect: the arguments/arguments-v3 schemas stop embedding the raw `validate_by_name` config key and instead embed the value after the `populate_by_name` and `validate_by_alias=False` compatibility mapping. All eight independent tests, covering both the `populate_by_name` case and the `validate_by_alias=False` variant, fail on base and pass on both patches, so correctness on the issue's scenarios is equal.

Tests separate them. Patch B adds tests for both variants the issue describes (`populate_by_name=True` and `validate_by_alias=False`), parametrized across both `arguments` and `arguments-v3` schema types in the experimental module, plus a `validate_call` test that also checks alias behaviour per config and a negative `populate_by_name=False` test. Patch A only tests `populate_by_name=True`, only for `arguments-v3` in the experimental test, and never exercises the 'worse variant' (`validate_by_alias=False`) that the issue explicitly calls out. A also includes unrelated `dict(...)` to `{...}` churn in three existing tests.

On craft, A has a point in its favour: it reuses `core_config()` as the single source of truth rather than duplicating the mapping logic, whereas B introduces `effective_validate_by_name`, which re-implements the compatibility rules and could drift from `core_config()`. B also widens scope by routing model and dataclass signature generation through the new property. That is a plausible adjacent fix (restoring pre-2.11 signature behaviour under `populate_by_name`) but it is untested and changes behaviour outside the issue's ask, so it earns no credit and carries mild risk.

Weighing in order: correctness is a wash, B's tests are materially stronger and directly cover the second reported failure mode, and the scope/craft trade-offs roughly offset (A's test churn and missing coverage versus B's duplication and untested signature change). B is the better patch.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Since v2.11, `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True))` no longer allows passing an aliased parameter by its name — the same config on a `BaseModel` works, and the [`populate_by_name` docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/config/#pydantic.config.ConfigDict.populate_by_name) say it is strictly equivalent to `validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True` (deprecated in v3, but still supported). Works on 2.10.6; broken on 2.11.x, 2.12.x, and `main`.

A worse variant: `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False))` makes the aliased parameter impossible to provide at all (both name and alias raise), even though #11503 made `validate_by_alias=False` implicitly enable `validate_by_name`.

Root cause: `_arguments_schema()`/`_arguments_v3_schema()` embed `validate_by_name=self._config_wrapper.validate_by_name` into the core schema (`_generate_schema.py:2081/2149`), reading the raw config key. The backwards-compatibility patch mapping `populate_by_name` → `validate_by_name` only runs inside `ConfigWrapper.core_config()`, and pydantic-core gives the schema-embedded value precedence over the validator config, so the patched core config is never consulted. Models are unaffected because model-fields schemas don't embed the flag.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, validate_call

@validate_call(config=dict(populate_by_name=True))
def f(a: Annotated[int, Field(alias='b')]) -> int:
    return a

f(b=1)  # OK
f(a=1)  # ValidationError: Unexpected keyword argument
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
             pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.14 (main, Oct  9 2025, 16:16:55) [Clang 17.0.0 (clang-1700.4.4.1)]
                     platform: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: 2151025
```

(also reproduced on released pydantic 2.11.10 and 2.12.5; not reproducible on 2.10.6)

title: validate_by_alias=False still produces a validation JSON schema keyed by the alias

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core change in `_get_alias_name`: when `validate_by_alias` is False in the current config, the validation schema uses the field name. That fixes the model, pydantic dataclass, and configured TypedDict cases, and both patches add regression tests covering the main scenario, serialization being untouched, and scoping between nested models. The independent tests confirm both pass those.

Patch A goes further where the same defect still exists after Patch B's one-liner. Config-less TypedDicts and stdlib dataclasses nested in a `validate_by_alias=False` model inherit the parent's core config, so validation of them really uses the field name, yet with Patch B their schema still names the alias (the independent test `test_validate_by_alias_false_nested_configless_types_follow_model` fails on B, passes on A). Patch A handles this by reading `validate_by_alias` from the core schema's `config` when pushing the config wrapper for typed-dict and dataclass schemas. It also covers named-tuple field titles, arguments schemas (`validate_call`/`TypeAdapter` of a function), and threads `validate_by_alias` into the generated arguments core schemas so the JSON schema can read it per schema rather than from an ambient config. These are not unrelated churn; they are the same 'schema names a key the validator rejects' bug in other containers the generator handles, and each path has a dedicated test.

Risk assessment: Patch A's added surface (a context manager for arguments schemas, a helper to merge core-config `validate_by_alias`) is small, clearly named, and consistent with the existing config-wrapper-stack pattern. The `_generate_schema.py` change only passes a setting that core already reads from config, so validation behavior should be unchanged. Patch B is minimal and correct for the headline case but leaves a real, reachable instance of the issue unfixed. Patch A wins on correctness and test coverage without meaningful added risk.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

With `validate_by_alias=False`, the validation JSON schema still names the alias — which is the one key the model refuses.

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False, validate_by_name=True)
    my_field: str = Field(alias='myAlias')

Model.model_json_schema()
#> {'properties': {'myAlias': ...}, 'required': ['myAlias'], ...}

Model(my_field='x')                          # accepted
Model.model_validate({'myAlias': 'x'})       # ValidationError
```

So the schema describes the opposite of the model: it requires the rejected key and omits the accepted one. `model_json_schema(by_alias=False)` produces the right document, but a caller has to know the model's config to know to ask for it.

### Why this looks like an oversight rather than a decision

`_get_alias_name` already picks the alias per mode, and it already returns the field name when no alias applies in that mode:

```python
elif self.mode == 'validation':
    alias = field.get('validation_alias', name)
else:
    alias = field.get('serialization_alias', name)
```

Which is visible in behaviour today:

| field | validation schema | serialization schema |
|---|---|---|
| `Field(serialization_alias='sAlias')` | `my_field` ✅ | `sAlias` ✅ |
| `Field(validation_alias='vAlias')` | `vAlias` ✅ | `my_field` ✅ |
| `Field(alias='myAlias')` + `validate_by_alias=False` | `myAlias` ❌ | `myAlias` |

The principle "use the alias only in the mode where it applies" is already implemented. `validate_by_alias=False` turns the validation alias off, and the generator simply does not consult it.

I have a fix and regression tests ready, and will open a PR without a closing reference so it does not trip `enforce-issue-assignment`.

### A related asymmetry I did not touch, because it is your call

`serialize_by_alias` defaults to `False`, so with nothing but a plain `Field(alias=...)` the serialization schema already disagrees with the default dump:

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    my_field: str = Field(alias='myAlias')

Model(myAlias='x').model_dump_json()
#> {"my_field":"x"}

Model.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties']
#> {'myAlias': ...}
```

By the argument above that is the same defect. But unlike `validate_by_alias=False`, which is an explicit opt-out affecting only the people who set it, `serialize_by_alias=False` is the default, so honouring it would change the serialization schema of **every** aliased model. That is a breaking change and a product decision, not a drive-by fix, so I have deliberately left it alone and am raising it here instead. Happy to follow up either way you decide.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError


class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False, validate_by_name=True)

    my_field: str = Field(alias='myAlias')


print(list(Model.model_json_schema()['properties']))
#> ['myAlias']

print(Model(my_field='x'))
#> my_field='x'

try:
    Model.model_validate({'myAlias': 'x'})
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(exc.errors()[0]['type'])
    #> missing
```

```Text

        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false

                     platform: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: d4e72fa
```

Patch B adds only pydantic-level tests, albeit with extra/reverse-order parametrization, and leaves an unfilled `<link>` docstring placeholder (stripped reference, ignored for scoring but still a stub). Both patches include an extra-fields hardening test that is neutral. Scope and craft are otherwise equal, so Patch A's two-layer test coverage, matched to the location of the fix, gives it a modest but real edge.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In the pipeline API, `multiple_of()` is broken for every temporal type. `timedelta` rejects **every** value, including exact multiples, and `date`/`time`/`datetime` raise a bare `TypeError` that escapes as-is instead of a `ValidationError`.

| annotation | `.multiple_of(...)` | `Field(multiple_of=...)` | correct |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `float` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `Decimal` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `Fraction` | predicate check | n/a (unsupported by core) | ✅ |
| `timedelta` | **rejects everything** | accepts | ❌ |
| `date` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |
| `time` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |
| `datetime` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |

`validate_as(timedelta).multiple_of(timedelta(seconds=5))` rejects `timedelta(seconds=10)`, which is an exact multiple.

### Root cause

`_apply_constraint()` applies `multiple_of` natively only for a hardcoded `{'int', 'float', 'decimal'}`, and otherwise falls back to a Python predicate:

```python
def check_multiple_of(v: Any) -> bool:
    return v % multiple_of == 0
```

That predicate cannot work for temporal types:

* `timedelta(seconds=10) % timedelta(seconds=5)` is `timedelta(0)`, and `timedelta(0) == 0` is `False` in Python. The check therefore never holds, for any input.
* `date`, `time` and `datetime` do not support `%` at all, so the predicate raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %`, which is not wrapped into a `ValidationError`.

This looks like an oversight rather than a decision. #13659 generalised exactly this pattern for the other constraints, introducing `_ORDERING_SCHEMA_TYPES` for `gt`/`ge`/`lt`/`le` and `_LENGTH_SCHEMA_TYPES` for `min_length`/`max_length`, both of which cover the temporal types. `MultipleOf` was left on its old hardcoded set in the same function.

Pydantic's own metadata already records the correct answer — `DATE_TIME_CONSTRAINTS` in `_known_annotated_metadata.py` includes `NUMERIC_CONSTRAINTS`, i.e. `multiple_of`:

```python
>>> from pydantic._internal._known_annotated_metadata import CONSTRAINTS_TO_ALLOWED_SCHEMAS
>>> sorted(CONSTRAINTS_TO_ALLOWED_SCHEMAS['multiple_of'])
['date', 'datetime', 'decimal', 'float', 'int', 'time', 'timedelta']
```

`fraction` is correctly absent there, and must keep using the predicate path — `fraction_schema()` takes no `multiple_of` argument, and `Fraction` supports `%` correctly.

### Suggested fix

Apply the constraint natively for the schema types that accept it, mirroring #13659:

```python
# Core schema types with native support for the `multiple_of` constraint:
_MULTIPLE_OF_SCHEMA_TYPES = frozenset({'int', 'float', 'decimal', 'date', 'time', 'datetime', 'timedelta'})
```

This aligns the pipeline API with the non-experimental API, per the position in #13564 that the two should agree. Note that this makes `multiple_of` a silent no-op on temporal types, because `pydantic-core` accepts the key but does not enforce it there — which is exactly what `Field(multiple_of=...)` already does today. Enforcing it would be a `pydantic-core` change and a separate discussion; this issue is only about the pipeline API diverging from `Field()`.

I have a fix and regression tests ready (the tests fail without the fix and pass with it, and `pyright` stays at its existing baseline). Happy to open a PR if I could be assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

td = datetime.timedelta

# 1. timedelta: an exact multiple is rejected.
ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[td, validate_as(td).multiple_of(td(seconds=5))])
ta.validate_python(td(seconds=10))
# ValidationError: Value error, Expected % 0:00:05 == 0
# (timedelta(0) == 0 is False, so the predicate never holds)

# 2. date/time/datetime: raw TypeError, not a ValidationError.
ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[datetime.date, validate_as(datetime.date).multiple_of(2)])
ta.validate_python(datetime.date(2020, 1, 1))
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %: 'datetime.date' and 'int'
```

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ValidateCallWrapper.__call__` is declared as `def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs)`, so the instance is bound to the name `self`. A decorated function with a keyword parameter literally named `self` can then never be called with it: `f(self=1)` raises `TypeError: ValidateCallWrapper.__call__() got multiple values for argument 'self'` before validation runs. The wrapped function itself is fine with that name; it is only the wrapper's signature that collides. Same in 2.12.5, 2.13.5 and `pydantic/_internal/_validate_call.py` on main.

Making `self` positional-only in `__call__` (`def __call__(self, /, *args, **kwargs)`) removes the collision without changing anything else. Can send the PR.

import pydantic.version
from pydantic import validate_call


@validate_call
def f(*, self: int) -> int:
    return self


try:
    print("f(self=1) ->", f(self=1))
except TypeError as e:
    print("f(self=1) -> TypeError:", e)
print(pydantic.version.version_info())
```

title: multiple_of=0 still raises ZeroDivisionError for non-native numeric types

judge.reasoning:
The issue identifies the root cause as the Python fallback in `_validators.py` doing `x % multiple_of` without validating the divisor, and names Fraction, temporal types, and complex as users of that fallback. Patch A fixes exactly that: it adds `check_multiple_of_constraint` and calls it at the fallback site in `apply_known_metadata` (and in the experimental pipeline's Python path), so every type routed through `multiple_of_validator` now fails at schema generation with the same message pydantic-core uses for int/float/Decimal. That covers Fraction, timedelta, complex, and also int/Decimal wrapped in function schemas (AfterValidator), with careful handling of Decimal('1e400'), huge ints, NaN/inf, and non-float types. Its tests are broad and would fail before the change (Fraction, timedelta, complex, int/Decimal function-schema, pipeline), and the test_types.py edit preserves the original intent of that test now that a 0 divisor is rejected earlier.

Patch B instead adds native `multiple_of` support to the Rust Fraction and Timedelta validators and reroutes those two types to core. That is a larger cross-repo feature (pydantic-core Rust + schema TypedDicts + a required core release) rather than a fix of the stated root cause. The unvalidated fallback remains: `complex` (explicitly named in the issue), int/Decimal under function schemas, and the pipeline still raise ZeroDivisionError. Its tests only cover Fraction and timedelta. Both patches pass the independent tests, but those tests only probe Fraction and timedelta, so they do not expose B's remaining gap.

A resolves the issue at its root with narrower, lower-risk scope and stronger tests; B masks the symptom for two types via a redesign and leaves the reported fallback problem in place for others.

issue_md:
### Description

`Field(multiple_of=0)` is rejected during schema generation for `int`, `float`, and `Decimal`, but equivalent non-native numeric types still pass schema generation and raise an uncaught `ZeroDivisionError` during validation.

### Reproduction

```python
from fractions import Fraction
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Model(BaseModel):
    value: Fraction = Field(multiple_of=0)

Model(value=Fraction(1, 2))
```

Actual: validation raises `ZeroDivisionError` rather than `ValidationError`.

Expected: model definition fails with a schema-generation error stating that `multiple_of` must be greater than zero, consistently with native numeric types.

The Python fallback in `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py` performs `x % multiple_of` without validating the divisor. `Fraction`, temporal types, and `complex` use this fallback. I found no existing report for the remaining types after the native numeric fix.

title: TypedDict `closed`/`extra_items` (PEP 728) not inherited by subclasses; `extra_items=Never` and `ReadOnly[...]` fail

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the three reported cases for plain inheritance, Never, and ReadOnly, and both pass 12 of 13 independent tests. The difference is generic parents: Patch B fails `test_extra_items_inherited_from_parametrized_generic_parent` (Child(Parent[int]) with extra_items=T), because B looks up `__extra_items__` through the virtual MRO of bare classes and discards the type arguments supplied in `__orig_bases__`, leaving an unsubstituted TypeVar. Patch A walks `__orig_bases__` directly, builds a per-base typevars map from the parametrization, and substitutes correctly; it also handles NoReturn as an alias of Never, protects against cycles, and respects an explicit `closed=False` on a subclass. Patch A's tests are substantially broader (grandchild, multiple bases, generic/parametrized parents, ReadOnly[Never], generic Never, inherited config warning). Patch B adds an unrequested UserWarning for ReadOnly extra items, which the PEP explicitly allows and the issue did not ask for, adding noise rather than value. A is the more correct and better-tested fix.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

PEP 728 support was added in #12179, but a few cases from the spec don't work.

1. `extra_items` isn't inherited. A subclass of a TypedDict with `extra_items=int`
should also accept extra int items. Pydantic treats the subclass as a plain TypedDict
and silently drops the extra keys.

2. `closed=True` isn't inherited. A subclass of a closed TypedDict should also reject
extra keys. Pydantic accepts them and drops them instead of raising `extra_forbidden`.

This also affects JSON schema: the parent gets `"additionalProperties": false`,
the subclass doesn't.

3. `extra_items=Never` and `extra_items=ReadOnly[int]` raise
`PydanticSchemaGenerationError`. The PEP says `extra_items=Never` is the same as
`closed=True`, and allows `extra_items` to be wrapped in `ReadOnly[]`.

For 1 and 2, I think the cause is that `_generate_schema.py` reads `__closed__` and
`__extra_items__` directly from the class. Per the PEP, those attributes only reflect
what was passed to that exact class, not its parents. TypedDict parents also aren't
in `__mro__`, only in `__orig_bases__`, so finding the inherited value means walking
those.

For 3, `extra_items` is passed straight to `generate_schema` without handling
`Never` or unwrapping `ReadOnly`.

I'd like to work on a fix for this if that's okay.

### Example Code

```Python
import json
from typing import Never

from typing_extensions import ReadOnly, TypedDict

from pydantic import TypeAdapter


class Parent(TypedDict, extra_items=int):
    a: str


class Child(Parent):
    pass


print(TypeAdapter(Parent).validate_python({'a': 'x', 'b': '1'}))
# {'a': 'x', 'b': 1}
print(TypeAdapter(Child).validate_python({'a': 'x', 'b': '1'}))
# {'a': 'x'}  expected {'a': 'x', 'b': 1}


class ClosedParent(TypedDict, closed=True):
    a: str


class ClosedChild(ClosedParent):
    pass


print(TypeAdapter(ClosedChild).validate_python({'a': 'x', 'b': 1}))
# {'a': 'x'}  expected ValidationError

print(json.dumps(TypeAdapter(ClosedParent).json_schema()))
# includes "additionalProperties": false
print(json.dumps(TypeAdapter(ClosedChild).json_schema()))
# missing "additionalProperties": false

TypeAdapter(TypedDict('TD', {'a': str}, extra_items=Never))
# PydanticSchemaGenerationError
TypeAdapter(TypedDict('TD', {'a': str}, extra_items=ReadOnly[int]))
# PydanticSchemaGenerationError
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.13.5
        pydantic-core version: 2.46.5
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.13.7 (tags/v3.13.7:bcee1c3, Aug 14 2025, 14:15:11) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]
                     platform: Windows-11-10.0.26100-SP0
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: unknown

Also reproduced on Linux with Python 3.15.0b4 and pydantic main (2.14.0b2).
```

+
+    The `__closed__` and `__extra_items__` attributes only reflect the arguments passed to the class itself,
+    so the value has to be looked up in the (original) bases if not specified.
+
+    Returns:
+        A two-tuple, containing whether the `TypedDict` is closed and the extra items type (`NoExtraItems` if
+            unspecified or if the `TypedDict` is closed). Type variables are replaced using `typevars_map`
+            (for the class itself) and by the arguments used to parametrize generic bases.
+    """
+    is_closed, extra_items = _find_typed_dict_extra_items(typed_dict_cls, typevars_map, set())
+    if not is_closed and not typing_objects.is_noextraitems(extra_items):
+        # Extra items can be marked as read-only, which has no impact on validation:
+        if typing_objects.is_readonly(get_origin(extra_items)):
+            extra_items = get_args(extra_items)[0]
+        # `extra_items=Never` is equivalent to `closed=True`:
+        if typing_objects.is_never(extra_items) or typing_objects.is_noreturn(extra_items):
+            is_closed, extra_items = True, typing_extensions.NoExtraItems
+    return is_closed, extra_items

+def _find_typed_dict_extra_items(
+    typed_dict_cls: Any, typevars_map: Mapping[Any, Any] | None, seen: set[Any]

+    if typed_dict_cls in seen:
+        return False, typing_extensions.NoExtraItems
+    seen.add(typed_dict_cls)
+
+    # `__closed__` is `None` when not specified:
+    closed = getattr(typed_dict_cls, '__closed__', None)
+    if closed:
+        return True, typing_extensions.NoExtraItems
+    extra_items = getattr(typed_dict_cls, '__extra_items__', typing_extensions.NoExtraItems)
+    if not typing_objects.is_noextraitems(extra_items):
+        return False, replace_types(extra_items, typevars_map)

+        return False, typing_extensions.NoExtraItems
